I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. I know the North China Plain — the soil here is deep alluvial loam, good for grain but the aquifer has been dropping for years. That weighs on me every time I open an irrigation valve.

I'm 62, my sons have moved to the city, so I'm managing 20 mu mostly alone with some seasonal hired help. The plan hasn't changed much in thirty years because the land and market haven't given me reason to change it: **winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same ground**. That's what this county does. That's what the soil is set up for. That's what the grain traders buy.

**Wheat (October planting):** I'll use Jimai 22 — an improved variety that's been reliable here for disease resistance and yield in our climate. I apply fertilizer in two passes: most of it worked into the soil before planting, then a topdress at jointing when the plant tells me it needs nitrogen. I've cut back to two irrigations — at jointing and heading — because I've seen neighbors drain their wells and I don't want that for my grandchildren's land. Three pesticide passes: a pre-emergence herbicide, a spring broadleaf application, and a combined fungicide-aphicide spray before harvest.

**Maize (June planting, same 20 mu):** I go straight in with no-tillage after the wheat combine rolls through — saves time and keeps moisture in. Zhengdan 958 hybrid, it's stable, the seed company supports it locally. Summer rains usually carry the maize through; I'll irrigate once at silking only if the forecast is dry. Maize doesn't need much hand-holding compared to wheat.

I'm not chasing maximum yield. I'm chasing reliable yield with manageable input costs and water use.

Fertilizer is applied in split doses to reduce runoff and match crop uptake. I deliberately limit wheat irrigation to two events — jointing and heading — because groundwater depletion in Hebei is a long-term threat I take seriously, and summer rainfall is usually sufficient for maize except at silking.
